script_blocks: On a small island off the coast of Alexandria, a fire has been burning at the top of a tower for longer than anyone alive can remember. Ships steer by it from far out at sea, where the coastline itself is too low and too dark to see. The tower is built in three tiers, each one narrower than the last, and it has stood there since the third century before our era.

It was built under Ptolemy the second, and the engineer who designed it, Sostratus of Cnidus, is said to have carved his own name into the stone beneath a layer of plaster bearing the king's name instead, so that when the plaster wore away, his name would be the one that lasted. Whether that story is true or invented later, it is the kind of thing people wanted to believe about the place.

The lighthouse survived for well over a thousand years, and then a sequence of earthquakes brought it down stone by stone across several centuries, until a fifteenth century sultan built a fort on the same spot, using the fallen blocks as its foundation. Somewhere under that fort, archaeologists believe, pieces of the tower are still waiting.
